{{Short description|Block cypher operating mode}}
[[File:Xor Encrypt Xor.svg|thumb|XEX technique: Key1 and Key2 extend the original (short) Key]]
The '''xor–encrypt–xor''' ('''XEX''') is a (tweakable) [[block cipher modes of operation|mode of operation of a block cipher]]. In tweaked-codebook mode with [[ciphertext stealing]] ([[Disk encryption theory#XTS|XTS mode]]), it is one of the more popular modes of operation for [[disk encryption theory#Xor–encrypt–xor (XEX)|whole-disk encryption]]. XEX is also a common form of [[key whitening]], and part of some [[smart card]] proposals.<ref>Barış Ege, Elif Bilge Kavun, and Tolga Yalçın. [http://emsec.rub.de/media/crypto/veroeffentlichungen/2012/01/16/mem_enc.pdf "Memory Encryption for Smart Cards"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103063122/http://www.emsec.rub.de/media/crypto/veroeffentlichungen/2012/01/16/mem_enc.pdf |date=2018-11-03 }}. 2011.</ref><ref>Emmanuel Prouff. [https://books.google.com/books?id=G2TlxEGwnzUC "Smart Card Research and Advanced Applications"]. 2011, p. 201.</ref>

== History ==
In 1984, to protect DES against exhaustive search attacks, [[Ron Rivest]] proposed [[DESX]]: XOR a pre-[[Key whitening|whitening]] key to the plaintext, encrypt the result with DES using a secret key, and then XOR a postwhitening key to the encrypted result to produce the final ciphertext.<ref name="DKS">[[Orr Dunkelman]], Nathan Keller, and [[Adi Shamir]]. [https://eprint.iacr.org/2011/541.pdf "Minimalism in Cryptography: The Even–Mansour Scheme Revisited"].</ref>

In 1991, motivated by Rivest's DESX construction, [[Shimon Even|Even]] and [[Yishay Mansour|Mansour]] proposed a much simpler scheme (the "'''two-key Even–Mansour scheme'''"), which they suggested was perhaps the simplest possible block cipher: XOR the plaintext with a prewhitening key, apply a publicly known unkeyed permutation (in practice, a [[pseudorandom permutation]]) to the result, and then XOR a postwhitening key to the permuted result to produce the final ciphertext.<ref name="DKS" /><ref>{{cite conference |last1=Even |first1=Shimon |last2=Mansour |first2=Yishay |title=A construction of a cipher from a single pseudorandom permutation |date=1991 |work= |book-title= |conference=Advances in Cryptology - ASIACRYPT '91: International Conference on the Theory and Application of Cryptology |location=Fujiyoshida, Japan |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |publication-place=Berlin, Heidelberg |isbn=9783540573326 |pages=210–224}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Even |first1=Shimon |last2=Mansour |first2=Yishay |title=A construction of a cipher from a single pseudorandom permutation |journal=Journal of Cryptology |date=June 1997 |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=151–161 |doi=10.1007/s001459900025}}</ref><ref>Joan Daemen, Laboratorium Esat. "Limitations of the Even–Mansour Construction". 1992. {{doi| 10.1007/3-540-57332-1_46}}</ref>

Studying simple Even–Mansour style block ciphers gives insight into the security of [[Feistel cipher]]s (DES-like ciphers) and helps understand [[block cipher]] design in general.<ref>Craig Gentry and Zulfikar Ramzan. [https://www.iacr.org/cryptodb/archive/2004/ASIACRYPT/218/218.pdf "Eliminating Random Permutation Oracles in the Even–Mansour Cipher"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810105414/https://www.iacr.org/cryptodb/archive/2004/ASIACRYPT/218/218.pdf |date=2017-08-10 }}. 2004.</ref>

[[Orr Dunkelman]], Nathan Keller, and [[Adi Shamir]] later proved it was possible to simplify the Even–Mansour scheme even further and still retain the same provable security, producing the "'''single-key Even–Mansour scheme'''":  XOR the plaintext with the key, apply a publicly known unkeyed permutation to the result, and then XOR the same key to the permuted result to produce the final ciphertext.<ref name="DKS" /><ref>
Orr Dunkelman; Nathan Keller; and Adi Shamir.
[https://www.iacr.org/conferences/eurocrypt2012/program.html "Eurocrypt 2012: Minimalism in Cryptography: The Even-Mansour Scheme Revisited"].
</ref>

In 2004, Rogaway presented the XEX scheme with key and location-dependent "tweaks":<ref name="rogaway_xex"/>

[[File:Xor Encrypt Xor (XEX) mode encryption.svg]]

Rogaway used XEX to allow efficient processing of consecutive blocks (with respect to the cipher used) within one data unit (e.g., a disk sector) for [[disk encryption theory#Xor–encrypt–xor (XEX)|whole-disk encryption]].<ref name="rogaway_xex">
{{cite web |last=Rogaway |first=Phillip |date=2004-09-24 |url=http://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/papers/offsets.pdf |title=Efficient Instantiations of Tweakable Blockciphers and Refinements to Modes OCB and PMAC}}</ref>

Many whole-disk encryption systems – [[BestCrypt]], [[dm-crypt]], [[FreeOTFE]], [[TrueCrypt]], [[DiskCryptor]], FreeBSD's [[Geli (software)|geli]], OpenBSD softraid disk encryption software, and Mac OS X Lion's [[FileVault]] 2 – support XEX-based tweaked-codebook mode with ciphertext stealing ([[XTS mode]]).
